newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN FINANCE CRIME UNIT HEAD THREATENS TO QUIT.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN FINANCE CRIME UNIT HEAD THREATENS TO QUIT.

text.p: The head of Belgium's specialised financial crime taskforce threatened on Tuesday to quit unless the unit was more than doubled in size.

The budget of the Central Office in the Fight Against Economic and Organised Financial Crime (OCDEFO/CDGEFID), which detected financial crime worth an estimated 148 billion Belgian francs between 1994 and 1996, was so tight its nine investigators had to pay their own mobile phone bills, director Jean-Pierre Doraene told a news conference.
"It's totally unacceptable," Doraene said. "I think we have showed that a service like ours is justified."
Doraene said the unit received 5.7 million francs when it was set up in 1993 in order to equip itself. By last year, this investment budget had been cut to 50,000 francs.
"I don't know what my budget is for 1997, or 1998...it's like flying a plane without a route," Doraene said.

According to the office's own statistics, 151 investigations into financial crimes were launched between 1994 and 1996, of which 87 were still underway. Only six were classified as without foundation.

The 151 cases related to 387 separate infractions, of which 178 were linked to organised financial crime, mainly money laundering. Other infractions related to drugs trafficking (70 cases), murder (34 cases), terrorism (two cases) and arms dealing (three cases), among other crimes.

Using data from 130 of the 151 cases, the unit estimated the crimes carried out were worth around 148 billion Belgian francs, of which more than 100 billion was the product of money laundering. Indirect tax frauds accounted for about 23 billion francs.
The unit helped in seizures in Belgium and abroad of drugs and cash worth an estimated 10 billion francs, or 7.1 percent of the estimated product of financial crimes.
Doraene appealed for the Belgian government to boost the unit's size from 18 to 58 staff, including specialised tax investigators, as advocated in a March 1994 law "that has never been implemented."
He noted the estimated 22 billion Belgian francs in value added tax fraud detected in the last three years would have cost the government about four billion francs.
Legislation to help in the fight against organised crime should also be adopted, including turning the burden of proof on its head so that suspects had to prove their assets were legal.

"It will be a catastrophe (if the measures are not carried out)," Doraene said. "If we don't get the means necessary I will have to consider that what we have done is not credible...and draw the conclusion that I am not the right man in the right place."
